insider_note: The parity check (even vs odd) is the standard first move whenever the limits are symmetric about zero — it either halves the work (even) or makes the whole integral zero (odd).

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Show the integrand is an even function
steps.margin_note: First mark. An even power of sine or cosine is always unaffected by x→−x.
steps.memory_tip: Even power + even power = even function — always confirm f(−x)=f(x) before halving the interval.

lines.text: whether the integrand is even or odd.

steps.why: Squaring sin(−x)=−sinx removes the sign, and raising cos(−x)=cosx to the fourth power also stays positive, so the whole product is unchanged under x→−x, which is exactly the definition of an even function.
common_mistakes: Checking only one factor's parity and not multiplying the two effects together.
Confusing 'even function' with 'even power' — they must be verified, not assumed.

steps.label: Double the half-range integral and evaluate
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both m=2 and n=4 are even, so Wallis's formula needs the π/2 factor before doubling.
steps.memory_tip: The integral over [−a,a] equals twice the integral over [0,a] when f is even — always prove this first.

lines.text: Wallis's formula, m = 2 and n = 4 both even:

steps.why: For an even function, the integral over a symmetric interval [−a,a] equals twice the integral over [0,a]; applying Wallis's mixed-power formula to sin²xcos⁴x (both powers even, so K=π/2) and doubling gives π/16.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to double the integral after establishing the function is even.
Missing the π/2 factor since both powers (2 and 4) are even.
